props.title: Foxes
props.initialSlug: Four teen girls navigate wild 1970s San Fernando Valley

sections.content: **Foxes** (1980) marked a pivotal moment in teen cinema, stripping away the glossy veneer typical of coming-of-age films to expose the raw reality of San Fernando Valley teenagers. Director Adrian Lyne's debut feature established his signature visual style - a gritty naturalism punctuated by dreamy, soft-focus moments that would later define **Fatal Attraction** (1987) and **9½ Weeks** (1986). Jodie Foster's nuanced performance as Jeanie anchors the film, coming right after her acclaimed work in **Taxi Driver** (1976), proving her seamless transition from child to adult roles.

sections.content: The film's unflinching portrayal of teenage drug use, sexuality, and disaffection influenced a wave of more realistic teen dramas in the 1980s. While **The Breakfast Club** (1985) would later polish these themes for mainstream consumption, **Foxes** kept its edge sharp, more closely aligned with the raw energy of **Kids** (1995) or **Thirteen** (2003). The film's soundtrack, featuring Donna Summer and Angel, perfectly captures the late-70s disco era's dying gasp.

Lyne's direction presents the San Fernando Valley as both paradise and prison, predating the similar geographic-social commentary of **Valley Girl** (1983) and **Earth Girls Are Easy** (1988). The film's treatment of female friendship and loyalty amid chaos would influence later works like **Ghost World** (2001) and **The Virgin Suicides** (1999). SUBHEAD: Impact on Teen Cinema

sections.content: **Foxes** helped establish a new template for teen films that prioritized authenticity over entertainment. Its DNA can be found in works like **Thirteen** (2003), **Spring Breakers** (2012), and **Mid90s** (2018) - films that refuse to soften their portrayal of teenage experience. The movie's influence extends beyond teen cinema into the broader American independent film movement, helping pave the way for directors like Gus Van Sant and Larry Clark.
